stem: Choose the word closest in meaning to “ephemeral”.
explanation: Ephemeral describes something that lasts only a very short time, so “brief” is the closest match. “Fragile” describes weakness, not duration.

stem: “Meticulous” most nearly means:
explanation: Meticulous means showing great attention to detail — the opposite of careless or hasty.

stem: “Ubiquitous” most nearly means:
explanation: Ubiquitous means found everywhere at the same time. Its opposite is rare.

stem: “Candid” is closest in meaning to:
explanation: Candid means honest and straightforward — frank. It is the opposite of deceptive.

stem: Choose the word closest in meaning to “benevolent”.
explanation: Benevolent means well-meaning and kindly; it comes from the Latin for “wishing well”. Wealth and strictness have nothing to do with it.

stem: “Diligent” most nearly means:
explanation: A diligent person works carefully and steadily. Intelligence is a different quality, and “lazy” is the opposite.

stem: “Lucid” is closest in meaning to:
explanation: A lucid explanation is clear and easy to understand. “Lucky” only looks similar; the two words are unrelated.

stem: Choose the word OPPOSITE in meaning to “frugal”.
explanation: Frugal means sparing with money. “Thrifty” is a synonym, so the opposite is “extravagant” — spending freely or wastefully.

stem: Choose the word OPPOSITE in meaning to “obsolete”.
explanation: Obsolete means no longer in use. “Outdated” and “ancient” are close in meaning to it; “current” is the opposite.

stem: In the sentence “The witness gave a terse reply,” the word “terse” means:
explanation: Terse describes speech that uses few words. It says nothing about anger, and it is the opposite of long and detailed.

stem: Neither of the clerks ______ ready for the audit.
explanation: “Neither” is singular, so it takes the singular verb “is”. The noun in the following phrase (“clerks”) does not change the subject.

stem: The number of applicants ______ increased this year.
explanation: “The number of” is singular, so it takes “has”. (“A number of applicants” would be plural and take “have”.)

stem: Which sentence is grammatically correct?

choices.text: She had gone to the office before the meeting started.
She had went to the office before the meeting started.
She had go to the office before the meeting started.
She has went to the office before the meeting started.

explanation: The past perfect is “had” plus the past participle “gone”. “Went” is the simple past and cannot follow “had” or “has”.

stem: It was the manager, not the clerks, who ______ late.
explanation: The relative clause attaches to “the manager”, which is singular, so “was” is correct. “Not the clerks” is parenthetical and does not control the verb.

stem: Each of the employees ______ required to submit a report.
explanation: “Each” is the subject and it is singular, so it takes the singular verb “is”. The plural “employees” sits inside the prepositional phrase and does not control the verb.

stem: Which sentence is grammatically correct?

choices.text: Between you and I, the plan will not work.
Between you and myself, the plan will not work.
Between I and you, the plan will not work.
Between you and me, the plan will not work.

explanation: “Between” is a preposition, so the pronouns after it take the object form: “you and me”. “Myself” is reflexive and needs an earlier “I” in the same sentence.

stem: If I ______ the supervisor, I would approve the request.
explanation: The sentence describes an imagined situation, which takes the subjunctive “were” in formal English: “If I were the supervisor…”.

stem: She is one of the clerks who ______ always on time.
explanation: “Who” refers to “clerks”, not to “one”: she belongs to the group of clerks who are always on time. A plural antecedent takes the plural verb “are”.

stem: The report, along with the receipts, ______ on the director’s desk.
explanation: Phrases such as “along with” and “as well as” do not make a subject plural. The subject is “the report”, so the verb is the singular “is”.

stem: Which sentence is grammatically correct?

choices.text: He do not knows the answer.

explanation: A third-person singular subject takes “does”, so the contraction is “doesn’t”, followed by the base form “know”.

stem: The new policy was ______ by employees, who welcomed the shorter queues.
explanation: The clause “who welcomed the shorter queues” tells us the reaction was positive, so the blank needs a positive word: embraced.

stem: Despite her ______ manner, she remained a fierce negotiator.
explanation: “Despite” signals contrast with “fierce”, so the blank must describe the opposite quality: mild.

stem: The hall was so ______ that even a whisper carried to the back row.
explanation: A whisper being audible across the room is only remarkable if the hall was very quiet.

stem: He was promoted not because he was the most brilliant, but because he was the most ______.
explanation: The “not … but …” construction sets up a contrast with brilliance, so the blank must name a different quality — steady effort, or diligence.

stem: The manager’s instructions were so ______ that no one knew what to do.
explanation: The result — no one knew what to do — points to instructions that were unclear. “Precise”, “helpful” and “detailed” would have the opposite effect.

stem: Because the evidence was ______, the case was dismissed.
explanation: A case is dismissed when the evidence is not enough to support it. Strong or convincing evidence would lead to the opposite outcome.

stem: The speaker’s ______ remarks offended many in the audience.
explanation: Remarks that offend people are thoughtless about their feelings — tactless. The other three words describe considerate speech.

stem: Although the task seemed ______ at first, it turned out to be quite simple.
explanation: “Although” signals a contrast with “quite simple”, so the blank needs a word meaning difficult or intimidating: “daunting”.

stem: The office adopted a ______ approach, testing the new system in one division before using it everywhere.
explanation: Trying something in one place before rolling it out is a careful, step-by-step choice. The other options describe the opposite.

stem: Her strict ______ to the rules earned her the respect of the auditors.
explanation: Auditors respect someone who follows the rules closely. “Adherence” means faithful compliance; the other words mean opposing or not caring about the rules.

stem: The barangay council approved an ordinance requiring stores to segregate their waste. Vendors first objected, citing the cost of extra bins. After the council offered free bins for the first year, compliance rose sharply. — What caused compliance to rise?

choices.text: Vendors were fined for not complying.
The council provided the bins at no cost.
Vendors changed the kind of goods they sold.

explanation: The passage states the objection was cost and that compliance rose after free bins were offered. Nothing in the passage mentions fines or withdrawal.

stem: The barangay council approved an ordinance requiring stores to segregate their waste. Vendors first objected, citing the cost of extra bins. After the council offered free bins for the first year, compliance rose sharply. — Which statement is supported by the passage?

choices.text: The council ignored the vendors' concerns.
Compliance remained low throughout the year.
Vendors opposed the ordinance mainly because of expense.

explanation: The only objection the passage reports is the cost of extra bins. The other options describe positions the passage never states.

stem: Many students assume that studying longer guarantees higher scores. Research on retrieval practice suggests otherwise: short, frequent self-testing often produces better retention than rereading notes for the same total time. — What does the passage suggest?

choices.text: How study time is used matters more than how much time is spent.
Rereading notes is the most effective method.
Self-testing only helps students who already score well.

explanation: The passage contrasts two methods given equal total time, so the distinguishing factor is how the time is used, not the amount.

stem: Many students assume that studying longer guarantees higher scores. Research on retrieval practice suggests otherwise: short, frequent self-testing often produces better retention than rereading notes for the same total time. — In the passage, “retention” most nearly means:

choices.text: The length of a study session

explanation: In this context retention is how much of the material the learner can keep and recall.

stem: A regional office introduced online booking for examination applicants. Before the change, applicants queued for hours, and many travelled far only to find that all slots were full. Now applicants choose a schedule from home and arrive only at their booked time. Some older applicants found the website hard to use, so the office kept a help desk for walk-in assistance. — What problem did online booking mainly address?
explanation: The passage describes hours of queuing and trips that ended with no slot available. It never mentions results, fees or rooms.

stem: A regional office introduced online booking for examination applicants. Before the change, applicants queued for hours, and many travelled far only to find that all slots were full. Now applicants choose a schedule from home and arrive only at their booked time. Some older applicants found the website hard to use, so the office kept a help desk for walk-in assistance. — Why did the office keep a help desk?

choices.text: A law required every office to have one.
Some applicants found the website hard to use.

explanation: The last sentence gives the reason directly: some older applicants found the website hard to use.

stem: A regional office introduced online booking for examination applicants. Before the change, applicants queued for hours, and many travelled far only to find that all slots were full. Now applicants choose a schedule from home and arrive only at their booked time. Some older applicants found the website hard to use, so the office kept a help desk for walk-in assistance. — Which statement can be inferred from the passage?

choices.text: The office did not expect every applicant to adjust to the online system.
All applicants preferred queuing in person.
The regional office closed after the change.

explanation: Keeping a help desk only makes sense if the office expected some applicants to struggle. Nothing in the passage supports the other three claims.

stem: Mangroves protect coastal communities by absorbing the force of waves during storms. Their dense roots also trap sediment, which keeps shorelines from eroding, and shelter young fish that local fishers later depend on. When mangroves are cleared for fishponds or construction, these benefits disappear, often long before the losses are noticed. — What is the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: Fishponds are more profitable than mangroves.
Mangroves give coastal areas several protective and economic benefits.
Storms are becoming stronger every year.
All construction along coasts should be banned.

explanation: Every sentence describes something mangroves do for the coast — storm protection, erosion control and fish nurseries — and what is lost without them.

stem: Mangroves protect coastal communities by absorbing the force of waves during storms. Their dense roots also trap sediment, which keeps shorelines from eroding, and shelter young fish that local fishers later depend on. When mangroves are cleared for fishponds or construction, these benefits disappear, often long before the losses are noticed. — According to the passage, how do mangroves prevent erosion?
explanation: The passage says the dense roots “trap sediment, which keeps shorelines from eroding”.

stem: Mangroves protect coastal communities by absorbing the force of waves during storms. Their dense roots also trap sediment, which keeps shorelines from eroding, and shelter young fish that local fishers later depend on. When mangroves are cleared for fishponds or construction, these benefits disappear, often long before the losses are noticed. — The phrase “often long before the losses are noticed” suggests that the damage from clearing mangroves is:

choices.text: Gradual and easy to overlook at first

explanation: If the benefits disappear before anyone notices, the harm builds up quietly — it is not immediate or obvious.

stem: PEN : WRITER :: NEEDLE : ______
explanation: A pen is the tool of a writer, so the needle is the tool of a tailor. “Thread” is used with a needle but is not the person who uses it.

stem: PUPPY : DOG :: CUB : ______
explanation: The relationship is young animal to adult animal. A cub is the young of a bear (or another large mammal).

stem: THIRSTY : DRINK :: TIRED : ______
explanation: The relationship is condition to its remedy. A thirsty person drinks; a tired person rests. A yawn is a sign of tiredness, not its remedy.

stem: DROUGHT : RAIN :: FAMINE : ______
explanation: Rain relieves a drought; food relieves a famine. Hunger is the condition itself, not the relief.

stem: DOCTOR : HOSPITAL :: TEACHER : ______
explanation: The relationship is worker to workplace: a doctor works in a hospital, and a teacher works in a school.

stem: HOT : COLD :: ABUNDANT : ______
explanation: The pairs are opposites. The opposite of abundant is scarce; “plentiful” is a synonym.

stem: FINGER : HAND :: PETAL : ______
explanation: The relationship is part to whole: a finger is part of a hand, and a petal is part of a flower.

stem: AUTHOR : NOVEL :: COMPOSER : ______
explanation: The relationship is creator to creation: an author writes a novel, and a composer writes a symphony.

stem: THERMOMETER : TEMPERATURE :: ODOMETER : ______
explanation: The relationship is instrument to what it measures. An odometer measures distance travelled; speed is measured by a speedometer.

stem: SEED : TREE :: EGG : ______
explanation: The relationship is early stage to mature form: a seed grows into a tree, and an egg hatches into a bird.
